turns: Thank you for coming. I will be direct: this congregation has been on this corner since 1979, and our parking lot fills up every Sunday and twice at Easter. Why should we give up any of it for a project we did not ask for?

I hear that, and I appreciate the honesty about counting cars. But our neighbors have fought every apartment proposal on this street for twenty years. What happens to our relationship with them when the first bulldozer shows up, and why is that our problem to carry?

Fair enough on the neighbors. My bigger worry is the land itself. Once homes are built on it, that land is never coming back to us. How do we keep any real say over what happens there in thirty years, and what stops this from becoming something we never agreed to?

Let me ask the question the finance committee will ask me. We have a roof that leaks and a budget that barely closes. Where does the money for studies, lawyers and construction come from, and what exactly are you asking us to put on the line?

You have given us more to think about than I expected. One last thing: our members are tired of promises that take a decade. If the board said yes in principle next month, what would actually happen in the first year, and when would the first family move in?
feedback:
What landed
- You led with the families, not the law. The board member softened the moment you described who would live in the homes and that they would own them.
- Offering to count cars on the busiest Sunday before any commitment turned the parking fight into a shared task.
- Naming the ministerial approval under SB 4 gave a believable reason the timeline is shorter than past proposals.

What to tighten
- Say early and plainly that title can stay with the congregation through a ground lease, and that the sanctuary is never part of the deal. The control question is the one that sinks these conversations.
- Add the Phase I environmental site assessment when liability comes up; it answers the risk question with a requirement, not a reassurance.
- Close each answer with a question back to the board, such as what must stay exactly as it is. It keeps the meeting a conversation instead of a pitch.

Nothing is decided in a first meeting. You earned the second one.
